initial_requirements: Vrije Universiteit Brussel needs a Publications Management System for storing bibliographic records and full publication texts. Users with different roles should be able to search, upload, download, correct, and moderate publication information according to their access rights. The system should extract bibliographic details from documents, support bulk imports, and help reconcile alternative names that refer to the same author or institution.

messages.content: Could you describe the different user roles involved in the Publications Management System and the main actions each role should be allowed to perform, especially for searching, uploading, correcting, moderating, and downloading publication records?

Yes, at a high level we expect a few different roles. Regular researchers or staff should mainly be able to search the publications, upload new records or full texts for their own work, and download records or documents they have access to. Editors or faculty admins would have broader rights to correct metadata, merge duplicates, and review uploads before they become visible more widely. Then there should be moderators or librarians who can approve, reject, or adjust publication information, handle exceptions, and manage author or institution name reconciliation. I’m not fully sure yet where the boundary should be between faculty admins and central library staff, so that part would need confirmation.

Could you define the access control model in more detail—for each role, what specific permissions should they have for viewing, uploading, editing, approving, rejecting, merging, and handling publication records, and are there any rules based on ownership, faculty, or publication status?

We’d want access to be tied both to role and to the scope of the record. In general, authors or contributors can view all public records and edit only the items they own or submitted, while faculty admins can edit records within their faculty and approve routine changes. Moderators or librarians should have the highest operational rights: they can approve, reject, merge duplicate records, and correct metadata across faculties when needed.
Ownership matters for draft or newly uploaded records, because the submitter should be able to revise them until they are approved. Once a record is published or approved, normal users shouldn’t overwrite it directly; they should create a correction request or a new version depending on the workflow. I’d also expect some status-based rules, like drafts being visible only to the owner and reviewers, approved records being broadly searchable, and rejected records staying hidden except for audit purposes.

Could you describe the publication status lifecycle you want the system to support—for example, the possible statuses a record should move through from draft or upload through review, approval, publication, rejection, correction, or replacement, and what triggers each transition?

We’d need a simple lifecycle with a draft or imported state first, where the record is created but not yet validated. Then it should move into review once a user submits it or a bulk import is processed, and at that point a moderator or librarian can either approve it, send it back for correction, or reject it if it is wrong or incomplete. Approved records become published and searchable for everyone with access, and if later corrections are needed, I’d expect either an updated version to replace the old one or a correction status that keeps the history. If a publication is superseded by a newer version, the old one should probably be marked as replaced rather than deleted, so we keep traceability.

When publications are brought in through bulk import or automatic bibliographic extraction, what validation checks should the system perform before a record is accepted—for example, required fields, format checks, duplicate detection, confidence thresholds, and whether low-quality or uncertain items should be rejected, queued for review, or routed to a specific role?

Before accepting an imported record, the system should check that the core bibliographic fields are present and valid, things like title, authors, year, and at least one identifier if available. It should also do format checks on dates, DOI or ISBN patterns, file types for uploads, and basic consistency between the extracted text and the metadata. Duplicate detection is important too, especially against existing records and alternative author or institution names.
For extraction confidence, I’d expect a threshold rule. High-confidence items could go straight into the review queue or even be auto-accepted for very simple cases, while low-confidence or incomplete records should not be published automatically and should go to a moderator or librarian for manual checking. If the quality is too poor, the system should reject the item or flag it as unusable rather than letting it clutter the database.
